Area.evidence_source: It was apparent from these men's stories that lack of disclosure around emotional difficulties was maintained even if individuals regarded themselves as having close relations with family and friends. However, other subjects detailed histories of social and psychological isolation from their own families, a separation which they themselves frequently nurtured. They often desired emotional engagement but felt unable to follow this through because an emotional discourse was unacceptable in the home and or because it went against their own expectations around masculinity.Gendered expectations around behaviour can also be shared by family and friends and this can present a further barrier to disclosure. Men can thus experience difficulties being heard when they do attempt to communicate distress. In some of the narratives it was clear that a major warning signal was ignored by family members. This reflected a deeper disconnection as some men had developed a lifestyle which was quite marginal to their families. Their objective in doing this was to create sufficient emotional distance to protect the self from unmasking. Work commitments were sometimes incorporated into this distancing operation. Social and emotional separation from wives and other partners reduced the protective possibilities ofthis environment, sometimes allowing even unusual behaviour to remain unchallenged.My whole life from the day I started work revolved around work. I loved it. For someone who spent all his teenage years or practically all of them on my own and then I went into a job where there were hundreds of people every day. When I was at school I started off as a lounge boy. If someone had said to me when I was 15 or 16 that I was going to be a barman I would have laughed at them but just one day the manager asked me did I want to become an apprentice and I said yeah. You can be in a pub with hundreds of people and yet you can still be on your own I mean from a working point of view because it is very false but I enjoyed it and I started drinking as well when I was 18 so that changed my humour to being more sociable to talk to people, not from the work front from the people I worked with. And that changed me outside work then for the better. It was years later that I drank too much. I am an alcoholic. I know. I could safely say that the first time I had a drink I was an alcoholic. I know that now but I didn't know it then. I didn't drink for the sake of drinking. I drank because it changed my humour and it made me more sociable. Of course then drinking had taken over. The reason why I was never at home most of the time was work and half of the rest of the time I was in the pub somewhere.But while family is the origin of basic trust for many, out-of-home relationships have become increasingly important in sustaining the selfin late or post modernity. Friendship was therefore another possible opportunity for the men to engage emotionally.
